We sum the weights of all vertices and edges in H and compare to k. This verification procedure runs in time polynomial in the size of the input graph and target value k. Therefore the problem belongs to the class NP, and we now proceed to show that it is also NP-hard via reduction. We reduce from the classical SUBSET SUM problem, which asks whether some subset of the given integers sums to exactly a target value k. Given an instance of SUBSET SUM with integers a1 through an and a target value k, we now construct a graph G that has the following structure. For each integer ai, we create a single vertex vi in the graph G with vertex weight equal to ai, and we do not add any edges to the graph. The target value for our GRAPH-WEIGHT problem is set to k, and the graph has exactly n vertices and zero edges, so any subgraph is simply a set of vertices with no edges. Any subgraph of G is therefore determined entirely by which subset of vertices we select, and its weight is simply the sum of the weights of all selected vertices, which corresponds exactly to a subset sum. Thus a subgraph of G has total weight k if and only if there exists a subset of the given integers a1 through an whose sum is exactly equal to k, which is precisely the SUBSET SUM decision question. The reduction clearly takes polynomial time since we only need to create n vertices with weights taken directly from the input integers and we do not add any edges to the graph, so the total output size is clearly linear in n. Since SUBSET SUM is a well-known NP-Complete problem and we have constructed a polynomial-time reduction from SUBSET SUM to GRAPH-WEIGHT, and since we have also shown that GRAPH-WEIGHT belongs to the class NP, we can now confidently conclude that the problem GRAPH-WEIGHT is indeed NP-Complete.
